Oṃ, homage to the Guru.
O Wielder of the Trident, show favor toward those men of meager wealth who do not perform the Agnihotra sacrifice; for them, grant the Prāṇāgnihotra.

In this body, how many fires are there? Who is the sacrificer? Who is the wife? Who is the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)? Who is the *adhvaryu*? Who is the *hotṛ*? Who is the *udgātṛ*? Who is the supervisor (*upadraṣṭṛ*)? Who is the one who gives the command (*pratiprastotṛ*)? Who is the *snātaka*? Who is Indra? Who are Indra and Agni? What is the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*)? What is the fuel (*indhana*)? What is the pitcher (*kalaśa*)? What is...?
The waters. What is the *argha*? What is the *argha*-vessel? (p.
250b) What is the fragrance? What is the flower? What is the incense? What is the lamp? What is the altar (*vedi*)?

What is the inner altar (*antarvedi*)? What is the fuel (*idhma*)? What are the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*)? What is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)? What is the sacrificial knife (*araṇi*)? And what is the level ground (*sama*)? What is it?

What is the sacrificial animal? What is the oblation? What is the tongue? What is the *upayāma* (the vessel for holding the Soma)? What are the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles? What is the *puroḍāśa* cake? What are the worlds (*bhuvana*)?

What are the realms (*loka*)? What are the intermediate spaces between the worlds? What does one offer as an oblation? Who are the *umā* deities who become gratified? O Blessed One, you ought to explain this reality of creation.
O Six-faced One, listen; I shall speak that most secret and supreme question which you have raised, which has not been told to anyone.
This supreme secret must not be given to just anyone;
rather, it should be bestowed only after examination upon one who worships the guru, the deity, and the fire.
In this body there are seven fires:
the Āhavanīya fire is in the mouth, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire resides in the mind,
the Gārhapatya fire is in the heart, and the Aupāsada fire is said to be in the navel.
The northern fire is between the eyebrows; the upward fire is at the distance of twelve finger-breadths [above the head];
the downward fire is between the feet—thus are the seven fires remembered.

Within these bodies, the person (*puruṣa*) is the sacrificer; primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the wife; the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); the upward-moving breath (*udāna*) is the assistant priest (*adhvaryu*); the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) is the invoker (*hotṛ*); the equalizing breath (*samāna*) is the chanter (*udgātṛ*); the in-breath (*apāna*) is the assistant chanter (*upagātṛ*); the pervasive breath (*vyāna*) is the supervisor (*draṣṭṛ*); the mind (*manas*) is the bath-graduate (*snātaka*); the self (*ātman*) is Indra; thirst (*tṛṣṇā*) is Indrāṇī; and the vehicle is the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).

The root mantra is fire; the rising of the sun is the oblation (*homa*); the head is the *droṇa* measure; the jar is blood and water; the hair is *darbha* grass; the Brahma-vein is the sacrificial pot (*sthālī*); the eight cities are the planets; and the teeth—

The *argha* offering: the skull-cup is the *argha* vessel; the supreme atoms are the oblation; the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the lamp. Its mantra is the flower; the wind is the fragrance; the name is the altar-ground (*vedī*); the tongue is the inner altar-ground (*antarvedī*). The bones are the fuel-sticks (*idhma*); the intestines are the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); the ears are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) is the incense; the power of life-force (*prāṇaśakti*) is the fire-drill (*araṇi*).
The two eyebrows are the *buddhi*; the *upayāma* is the eyes; the *puroḍāśa* is the mind; the sacrificial animal is consciousness; the two hands are the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles;
and the sense organs are the *hṛts* (heart-offerings).
If a learned man indeed performs the sacrifice according to this very sequence, [he attains success].
Then the thirty-three crores of gods remain unsatisfied.
He who knows this is a knower of the Vedas;
he is one who has maintained the sacred fires and is capable in both the rites for the gods and the rites for the ancestors.
Therefore, within this body, all deities are held to be the sacrificers.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the knowledge of the Self as taught by Śiva,
by which the wise are liberated from the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
In this body: Viṣṇu is in the two feet; the Maruts are in the two calves; the Earth is in the two knees; Mitra and Varuṇa are in the two thighs; Indra and Agni are in the waist;
the Devas are in the anus; Bhadra is in the penis; Aśva is in the bones; Kuvīra is in the head; [and] Nāḍī is in the channels.

Agni [is located] in the stomach; the ocean in the intestines; the Nāgas in the entrails; Hari in the two sides; the ancestors on the back; merit and demerit on the two lips; Tvaṣṭṛ at the tip of the nose; Vāyu in the two arms; Kālarātri in the neck; Indra in the two hands; Krodha in the palms of the hands; the serpents in the fingers; and [the gods] in the nails.
The constellations. On the tongue is Sarasvatī; on the jaws is Guru; on the right fangs is Yama; on the left fangs is Bṛhaspati; on the teeth are the Maruts; and in the eyes are the Moon and the Sun.
The directions are in the two ears; the two Aśvins are in the two nostrils; all the limbs and sub-limbs are in the heart;
Nārāyaṇa is between the eyebrows; Maheśvara is in the head; above him is the Unmanifest (Avyakta).
The three essential millions of body hairs become the stars. Herein, from the navel up to the end of the head—

As for the seven worlds that have been described, the Bhūrloka is in the channel (nāḍī); the Bhuvarloka is in the heart; the Svarloka is in the throat; the Maharloka is in the stomach; and the Satyaloka is in the head.
Ābhāsatala is at the ankles, Śrītala at the knees, and Nabhastala at the shins;
below the channels (nāḍī) is Latābhāsa, and in the secret region (guhya) is that known as Bhūtāla;
Śrītala is in the region of the thighs, and Rasātala in the region of the ankles.
And likewise, from his two feet, there arose the seven regions known as the Pātālas.
Jambūdvīpa is sleep; Vyati is known as youthfulness; Kuśadvīpa is the element of consciousness (ciddhātu); and Krauñcadvīpa is the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti).
The island of Siṃhala is the unsubdued mind; the one known as Puṣkara is the intellect (manas);
and Śākala is the faculty of discernment (buddhi)—thus are the seven islands declared.
O Six-faced One, listen as I describe how seven rivers reside within this very body while it remains seated in its natural state.
The Gaṅgā is said to be on the head, and the Sindhu on the forehead; the Vitastā is at the tip of the nose, and the Śatarudriya should be at the throat;
the Yamunā is said to be in the heart, and the Sarasvatī in the channel.
The Airāvatī should be at the secret place, and the Vipāśā is situated below that.
Now listen: this body indeed consists of all sacred fords (tīrthas). At the aperture of Brahmā is the Brahma-tīrtha, and Kedāra is situated on the head.
Vārāṇasī is on the forehead, and likewise Puṣkara is in the heart;
Nāḍī and Aṅkanakhala are in the channels, and all sacred fords (tīrthas) reside within the self.
Brahmāvarta is in the right hand; these are the sacred sites (tīrthas) for embodied beings.
Beyond that are Devatīrtha, Pitṛtīrtha, and Vāyutīrtha.
The Soma-tīrtha and Agni-tīrtha are always situated within the body;
the tīrtha of truth, the tīrtha of compassion, and the tīrtha of restraint of the senses [are likewise internal].
One should not consider any other sacred ford superior to the sacred ford of compassion for all beings;
for that ford where the inner disposition is indeed stainless is the highest of all sacred fords.
p. 255a) Relying upon Mount Meru in the heart, the moon and the sun abide;
that which is intellect (buddhi) is the sun, and that which is mind (manas) is the moon.
Fire, as well as the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the gods, the sense organs, and the organs of action—
the self indeed consists of all the gods and likewise consists of all sacred fords (tīrtha).
Therefore, with every effort, one should always worship that which resides within the self;
for those who do not worship the self are like those by whom oblations are offered into themselves.
Those of deluded intent and evil conduct, who take delight in other gods,
do not know that Lord, the all-pervading Sovereign.
"O Six-faced One, it is true that they are indeed like beasts by birth;
one should not worship a linga made of clay, nor one of stone, nor one of gold."
One should worship the *liṅga* born of the body, which bestows the fruits of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
The *liṅga* is the abode within one's own body, wherein the mind itself is the Lord.
One should worship the Liṅga there in the center of the pericarp within the heart-pīṭha;
this is the auspicious pīṭha in the heart-pīṭha, adorned with all kinds of jewels.
Upon knowing this, after six months, there shall be the destruction of all sins;
one must not eat outside of the maṇḍala, nor indeed with the left hand.
One should never eat while naked or with the hair-tuft (śikhā) untied;
for Viṣṇu, Soma, Sūrya, Agni, and Śacīpati [are present therein].
They subsist upon the maṇḍala; therefore, one should construct a maṇḍala.
For the Asuras, Yātudhānas, and Rākṣasas of cruel deeds [subsist] upon it.
For they destroy the strength of food that is devoid of the *maṇḍala*;
they prepare *maṇḍalas* that are square or triangular.
O Bull among Sages, the two stages are the extensive measure;
having become one whose nails are pared by a nail, he seeks a disease with wood.
With a stone there would be loss of wealth; with an earthen vessel, there would be strife.
Hereafter, I shall explain the knowledge of the Self according to the prescribed method;
by knowing which, a living being is liberated from the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
One should purify the vessel with the Astra-mantra and offer the seat with the Praṇava;
the wise one should contemplate the entire body as having the form of the Haṃsa.
One should purify the sacrificial pit situated in the region of the heart by means of the *praṇava* alone;
for within that pit of the Moon, Sun, and Fire resides the supreme light in the center.
O lady of virtuous vows, the god who is the syllable *haṃsa* is the Jīvāditya;
where, accompanied by the mass of flames, he illuminates the navel-mandala.
This flame is the primary [element] of this [deity]; it always protects the tip of the tongue. This digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) should be meditated upon as the purifier (pāvaka), the Supreme Lord.
Having milked the cow of Anaṅga while concentrated at the dvādaśānta,
one should offer the five oblations beginning with prāṇa into the fire.
Having gathered that [nectar] into the vessel, one should not purify it by means of *recaka* (exhalation);
rather, O Six-faced One, one should contemplate that form of Soma by means of *pūraka* (inhalation).
This [line] is remembered as the nourisher; then, with a full [handful] or with *kuśa* grass, the Brahmin who desires success in his rites should scrape away the defects.
Hereafter I shall explain the sixteen kalās.
Within the center of the mouth, there is the junction (sandhi) where the svāhā and nairāhutī [mantras] reside.
One should meditate upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the center of the navel, with the mouth as the fire and the nether regions as the girdle;
situated in its center is the light, the all-consuming fire of Śiva.
When the body, possessing a garland of flames, is dissolved within the lotus-casket,
the seventy-two thousand channels are proclaimed.
Food is Soma, the two hands with the sacrificial ladle are the giver, and the Sun shall worship Hari;
having established himself in Brahmic concentration, he indeed partakes of the fourfold food.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—
these are the five vital airs within the bodies of embodied beings.
Having bowed to the heart as the seat of apāna and again to the anus;
samāna resides in the region of the navel, and udāna is situated in the throat.
The fifth among them is to be known as Vyāna, located in all the joints of the limbs.
One should offer food into these and consecrate the body of the twice-born with mantras.
When these [vital airs] are satisfied, they lead the fourfold food—white, yellow, digested, and uniform—to its respective places.

The *samāna* is the measure of the instrument-self (*karaṇātman*), or it is the measure established through placement. That which is called *udāna* is the impeller of hiccups, the sound, the expansion of the body, coughing, and upward departure.
Why is it called *vyāna* because it moves upward?
Because it initiates the actions of spreading, contracting, leaping, jumping, walking, calming, exertion, laughing, singing, dancing, playing musical instruments, and desire.
Because it pervades (*vyāpanāt*) or because it spreads out (*vyāyāt*), it is called *vyāna*.
For *prāṇa* has the sun as its deity;
*vyāna* has Viṣṇu as its deity—thus the deities are distinct.
One should diligently perform the Prāṇāgnihotra according to the prescribed rules;
liberated from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Whatever food one eats with a concentrated mind according to this rule,
by that being satisfied, the deities together with the ancestors are satisfied.
All deities reside in the heart; the vital breaths are established in the heart;
the twenty-four principles and the Supreme Puruṣa are in the heart.
One should know that the heart is located six finger-breadths below the throat, above the navel and below the lower part; it is the great abode for the dissected [body].
The fire that is satisfied is indeed one, yet it abides in seven ways;
by it the three worlds are pervaded, and thus the exponents of Brahman worship.
Nala is beneficial to all beings, from Brahmins down to dog-cookers;
one should offer these oblations to him, and they shall find satisfaction even with half a portion.
